clue.text: Ultimately, Katie Hopkins cuts off support for the poor

indicators.note: Taken ultimately, a name is reduced to the single letter it finishes on rather than the whole of it.
Milk goes off when it turns bad, and letters that have gone off will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: The final letter of Katie joins the shuffle.
Eleven letters of fodder, taken with the E.

explanation.surface: A newspaper columnist is being blamed for slashing the help available to people with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Katie Hopkins is a British newspaper columnist notorious for hard-hearted remarks about the poor, so the sentence reads as a headline about welfare cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A soup kitchen hands out free meals to people who cannot afford food, so a row of them is support for the poor.

clue.text: Filter air – not at home

blocks.note: To air a programme is to screen it — both are broadcasters' verbs.
Someone not at home is out.

explanation.surface: Purifying the air in a house while nobody is in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' wants to be the stuff being filtered, the object of the sentence; the wordplay needs it as the verb a television schedule uses.
explanation.definitionFit: To screen something out is to filter it: a screen sifts what may pass and holds the rest back.

clue.text: Fail to warm up sufficiently before start of game – one’s likely to lose

indicators.note: What stands before something stands ahead of it, so this chunk is written down first.
The start of a word is the single letter it opens on, not the whole word.

blocks.note: To do food is to cook it, so to cook it too little is to underdo it.
Only the initial letter of the word is wanted.

explanation.surface: A player skimps on the warm-up and walks out onto the pitch cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm up' is doing two jobs: the surface has an athlete stretching, the wordplay has food that has not been cooked enough.
explanation.definitionFit: An underdog is the competitor everyone expects to be beaten, named by their prospects rather than by their form.

clue.text: Before artist put on the canvas new religious work

indicators.note: A thing set before another stands in front of it, so this chunk leads the assembly.

blocks.note: A boxer put on the canvas has been knocked out, which the record books write as KO.
An artist may be a Royal Academician, RA after the name.
N is the standard abbreviation for new.

explanation.surface: A painter is flattened in front of his easel before starting a fresh commission.
explanation.walkthrough: The canvas is two canvases — the painter's cloth in the surface, the floor of the ring in the wordplay — and 'artist' pulls hard towards the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Koran is the scripture of Islam, and 'work' is the crossword's usual way of naming a book or composition without saying which kind.

clue.text: Feel sad? Come in

blocks.note: To feel something is to touch it.
Someone sad is down, low in spirits.

explanation.surface: A miserable friend is standing on the doorstep and being waved inside.
explanation.walkthrough: An aircraft told to come in is being brought onto the runway, which is the sense the definition needs; the surface offers hospitality instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane comes in when it lands, and to touch down is exactly that moment of the wheels reaching the ground.

clue.text: Beating from punch, getting cut before sound of the bell

indicators.note: A word getting cut comes up short, losing the letter it ended on.
Standing before the other piece means standing ahead of it, so these letters come first.

blocks.note: A punch is a hit, and the cut takes its last letter away.
A bell goes ding.

explanation.surface: A boxer takes a punch and is cut open just as the round ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word belongs to the ring — the punch, the cut, the bell — and the definition lives there too, so nothing in the sentence looks like an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiding is a thrashing, as in giving someone a hiding, so it matches 'Beating' as one noun for another.

clue.text: Rugby Union club having straight rugby posts?

blocks.note: A drink taken straight is taken neat, with nothing added to it.
The setter uses the word twice; here it only says which posts are meant, and hands over no letters.
A set of posts is two uprights joined by a crossbar — the shape of the letter.

explanation.surface: A rugby club is admired for the perfectly upright posts at either end of its pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Neath is a town in south Wales whose side is one of the oldest in Welsh rugby, so the definition is a place name serving as a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Neath RFC is a long-established Welsh rugby union club, so the answer is one particular club standing under the general description.

clue.text: Perhaps copper maintains good power – it might retain output from battery for consumer

definitions.text: it might retain output from battery for consumer

indicators.note: To maintain a thing is to keep hold of it, so these letters close around the piece named next.

blocks.note: 'Perhaps' flags an example, which is written eg.
G is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report.
Copper's chemical symbol is Cu.
P is the physicist's symbol for power.

explanation.surface: A police officer keeps a firm grip on power and on whatever the battery is putting out for the customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is a policeman on the surface and the metal in the wordplay, and 'battery' pulls the same trick with electricity and hen sheds.
explanation.definitionFit: An eggcup holds a boiled egg upright at the table, and eggs are what battery hens produce for whoever eats them.

clue.text: Pretty certain con is set-up – sucker not Yankee

indicators.note: In a down clue, something set up has been stood on end, so its letters are read from the bottom.
Saying a thing is not something takes that named letter out of the word in front.

blocks.note: A con is a do — a swindle — stood on its head.
A Dyson is the British vacuum cleaner that sucks, one letter lighter.
Yankee is Y in the radio alphabet, and that is the letter removed.

explanation.surface: A confidence trick is exposed, and the mug caught up in it turns out not to be American.
explanation.walkthrough: Dyson is the British make of vacuum cleaner, which is the joke buried in 'sucker', and the radio alphabet supplies the Yankee that has to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A bet quoted odds-on is judged more likely to happen than not, and the phrase carries over to anything you would confidently expect.

clue.text: Pierced from stab and stained with blood

blocks.note: A stab at something is a go at it, an attempt.
Blood stains what it touches red.

explanation.surface: A stabbing has left the victim and everything round them covered in blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stab' is the attempt rather than the knife — as in having a stab at it — and that everyday sense is the one the violent surface hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Gored is what a bull's horn does to whoever it catches, so it is pierced with a point driven right through.

clue.text: Way to write cards after game of golf

indicators.note: Coming after the other piece puts these letters behind it rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: A game of golf is a round.
The cards you are dealt are your hand.

explanation.surface: Somebody deals a hand of cards in the clubhouse once the golf is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface keeps everything at the golf club, where a round and a hand are both unremarkable, and nothing points at penmanship until the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundhand is a style of penmanship with rounded, evenly formed letters, so it is literally a way to write.

clue.text: Check – moving over knight, one might give away rank

indicators.note: Letters that are moving have left their places, so they arrive in a different order.

blocks.note: Ch. is the old chess notation for check.
The four letters of over, shifted into a new order.
A knight is N on the chessboard.

explanation.surface: A chess player escapes check by moving over the knight and betrays their standing in the game.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess supplies both short pieces — ch. for check, N for the knight — and 'rank' is a row of the board on the surface and a soldier's stripe in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chevron is the V-shaped stripe worn on a sleeve, and counting them tells anyone what rank the wearer holds.

clue.text: Hotel food around midday, that’s left out, curls up

indicators.note: A piece marked out is taken away from the letters rather than added to them.

blocks.note: Hotel is H in the radio alphabet.
Lunches are the meals eaten around midday, with the L gone.
Left is L, and that is the letter dropped.

explanation.surface: A hotel serves lunch at noon and something has been left off the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: The seam is hidden by the comma: 'that's left out' reads as food nobody wanted, and it is the instruction to lose a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hunches curls their shoulders up and forward, so 'curls up' describes the same movement of the body.

clue.text: A Spice Girl over making comeback around fiery studio session

indicators.note: A comeback is a return along the way it came, so these letters are read the other way round.
Going around something means closing over it, so the piece named next sits inside.

blocks.note: Victoria Beckham was Posh Spice, and she opens up to take the next piece in.
Something fiery is hot.
Over in the sense of excessively is 'too', turned back to front.

explanation.surface: A Spice Girl returns to the limelight for a heated session in front of the cameras.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh Spice is Victoria Beckham; the harder word is 'over', standing in for 'too' in the sense it carries in over-eager.
explanation.definitionFit: A photoshoot is the booked session in which a photographer works through a set of pictures, usually in a studio.

clue.text: Not initially bad weather for swimming in spring?

indicators.note: 'Not initially' strikes out the letter the next word begins on.
Letters swimming have drifted loose and wash up in an order of their own.

blocks.note: Without the B it opens on, the phrase leaves exactly nine letters to be rearranged.
B is the initial letter that goes.

explanation.surface: The weather was fine enough at first for a swim, back in the spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' reads as the season right through the sentence, and the definition needs it as a place where water comes out of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A headwater is the stream at a river's source, which is what a spring is — water rising at the top of the system.

clue.text: Restrain having thrown a punch

indicators.note: Something thrown away is gone, so the letter named after it is no longer in the word.

blocks.note: To restrain is to chain, and the A has been thrown out of it.
The single letter A is what leaves.

explanation.surface: One fighter is being held back after landing a blow.
explanation.walkthrough: To chin someone is British slang for hitting them on the jaw, so the definition is a verb and 'Restrain' at the front is the wordplay, not the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To chin a person is to punch them on the jaw, the slang verb matching 'punch' used the same way.

clue.text: Romeo during passion done in a flash

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so this letter drops in among the others.

blocks.note: Passion is heat, the metaphor English reaches for with strong feeling.
Romeo is R in the radio alphabet.
Someone done in is beat — worn out.

explanation.surface: Romeo, caught up in a passionate affair, is worn out in no time at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo is R in the radio alphabet, and 'done in' wants 'beat' in its slang sense of exhausted rather than the murderous one the surface hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In a heartbeat' is the idiom for doing something instantly, so a heartbeat stands for the flash of time it takes.

clue.text: Ocean vessel docked for a major route

indicators.note: A docked tail is a shortened one, so the word loses the letter at its end.

blocks.note: The main is an old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main.
A vessel is a liner, minus its final letter.

explanation.surface: A ship has tied up at the quay after crossing the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' does both jobs at once, berthing the ship in the surface and shortening the liner in the wordplay, while 'ocean' asks for the poets' word for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A mainline is the principal railway route between big cities, as against the branch lines that feed into it.

clue.text: Saucy thing admits backside in miniskirt sticks out

indicators.note: To admit something is to let it in, so these letters open up and take the next piece inside.
The backside of a word is the letter sitting at the very end of it.

blocks.note: A jus is a thin sauce, so it is a saucy thing indeed.
The letter the word ends on.

explanation.surface: Someone risqué is showing off the back of a very short skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy thing' plays as a flirt in the surface and as cookery in the wordplay — a jus is the pan juices poured over the meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To jut is to project outwards from a surface, which is what sticking out means, and both are third-person verbs here.

clue.text: Biblical figure formed from rib inspiring epistle

indicators.note: To inspire is to breathe in, so the word draws the piece named next inside itself.

blocks.note: To rib someone is to josh them, teasing rather than wounding.
Ep. is the standard short form of epistle.

explanation.surface: A Bible character is made out of a rib while an apostle's letter is read aloud.
explanation.walkthrough: The rib is Adam's on the surface, which points hard at Eve; in the wordplay it is a verb, and to rib is to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph is a Bible name twice over — Jacob's son with the coat, and the carpenter of the nativity — so either one answers to 'Biblical figure'.

clue.text: Nothing from lover, as many desperate to pick up date

indicators.note: People in a desperate state are all over the place, and so are the letters standing beside the word.
Picking a thing up gathers it in, so the letter named next joins the ones being shuffled.

blocks.note: A lover of a singer or a team is a fan.
Six letters of the shuffle, before the date joins them.
D is the everyday abbreviation for date.

explanation.surface: A hopeful suitor gets no reply at all from the person they are trying to arrange an evening with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet Fanny Adams' is British slang for nothing whatever, and it began as a grim Victorian joke about tinned meat named after a murder victim.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Adams, usually with 'sweet' in front, means nothing at all — the polite version of a much ruder phrase with the same initials.

clue.text: They hold balls in opening of Royal Ascot racing

indicators.note: The opening of a word is the single letter it starts on.
Letters racing are running about, and they cross the line in a different order.

blocks.note: The initial letter of the word.
Five letters of fodder, taken with the R.

explanation.surface: The first race of the week is under way at Royal Ascot.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Ascot is Britain's grandest and most formal race meeting, so 'opening of Royal Ascot' reads as the first day of it rather than as one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrota is the plural of scrotum, the sac that holds the testicles, so the plural definition points at more than one owner.

clue.text: Body in zone for running during training

indicators.note: A thing done during a session is done in the middle of it, so these letters sit inside.

blocks.note: PT is physical training, what British schools call the gym lesson.
A runner's own zone on the track is their lane.

explanation.surface: An athlete keeps strictly to their own lane during a training session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' is not the athlete's body the surface is describing but a heavenly one, which is the only word in the clue that leaves the running track.
explanation.definitionFit: A planet is a heavenly body, and 'body' alone is the astronomer's ordinary word for anything of that kind in orbit.

clue.text: Typical bits of grass, garden getting trimmed

definitions.note: The definition is the exclamation 'Typical!' rather than a noun matching the answer: the setter is defining the phrase by the word a British speaker says at the moment it strikes.

indicators.note: A hedge getting trimmed comes back shorter, and so does this word — the letter on the end goes.

blocks.note: Squares of turf cut out of a field are sods.
The grassy part of a garden is the lawn, with its final letter cut off.

explanation.surface: Somebody is out cutting turf and tidying the edges of the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Sod's law is the British name for Murphy's law — whatever can go wrong will — and 'Typical!' is what people actually say when it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Sod's law is invoked at exactly the moment someone groans 'Typical!', so the exclamation names the principle by the reaction it produces.

clue.text: Criticise old following Conservative Party

indicators.note: What follows another piece is written after it, so this letter takes the later place.

blocks.note: To dis someone is to criticise or disrespect them.
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative.
O is the standard abbreviation for old.

explanation.surface: A veteran Tory grandee is being attacked by his own side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative Party' looks like one phrase and the split falls between its two words — the party at the end is the dancing kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a party where records are played for dancing, so 'party' is the social sense rather than the political one the surface offers.

clue.text: Check dipstick in car? No time

indicators.note: 'In' is the plainest container instruction there is: what is in something sits inside it.
Saying no to a thing refuses it entry, so the letter it names is not in the word.

blocks.note: A car is a motor, and the T has gone from it.
A dipstick is British slang for a fool, and so is a nit.
T is the abbreviation for time, and that is the letter refused.

explanation.surface: A driver in a hurry checks the oil level before setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dipstick' is the oil gauge in the surface and an idiot in the wordplay, which is a piece of slang a garage sentence can hide completely.
explanation.definitionFit: To monitor something is to keep a check on it, watching it steadily to see how it changes.

clue.text: Old singer, ace, supporting Spice Girl

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever is supporting the rest sits underneath it, so this letter comes last.

blocks.note: Melanie Brown of the Spice Girls was billed as Mel B.
A is the standard abbreviation for ace.

explanation.surface: A great singer of the old days is reduced to opening for a Spice Girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Peach Melba and Melba toast are both named after Dame Nellie, which is how well known the singer the definition wants once was.
explanation.definitionFit: Nellie Melba was the reigning operatic soprano either side of 1900, so 'Old singer' places her by period rather than by voice.

clue.text: Last panto rearranged after infant pulled out

indicators.note: Something rearranged keeps all its parts and changes their arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: These nine letters are exactly the ones required, in a different order.

explanation.surface: The final pantomime of the season has been reorganised since a child dropped out of the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulled out' reads as a young performer leaving the show, and the definition needs it as a delivery — the baby is out and the clock starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Postnatal means belonging to the time after a birth, which is the stretch that begins once the infant has been delivered.

clue.text: Awkward to write about boring sex

indicators.note: Turning about faces a word the other way, so its letters are read from the end back.
To bore is to drive a hole into something, so these letters end up inside the other piece.

blocks.note: 'It' is the old euphemism, as in a film star having it.
To write is to pen, turned about.

explanation.surface: A clumsy novelist keeps writing about sex that bores everybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like a verdict on the writing and is an instruction instead — one word bores its way into another.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone inept is clumsy and unskilled, awkward in the sense of being no good at the task rather than of feeling embarrassed.

clue.text: Guardian fellow sent a report for editing

indicators.note: Editing a piece of copy moves its parts about, so the letters come out in a fresh order.

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for fellow.
Eleven letters of fodder, taken with the F.

explanation.surface: A man at the newspaper has filed his copy and the subeditors are working it over.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital G does the misdirecting: 'Guardian' reads as the paper the clue was printed in, and it means someone with legal care of a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A foster parent takes a child who is not theirs into their home and care, which is the job a guardian does.
